title: Recording habits with Oliver
summary: Takes ran three to four hours, unpaid overtime; Oliver preferred to rehearse in the studio.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: How much time did you have to make those four sides? Did you have to make those four sides in, say, a three-hour period? Or was it that you'd just go in and make the four sides and that was it?

Sometimes... Our first recording at Victor, we did it in, say, two days, which is... Sometimes... We did some of them in three hours, some in four hours. But they had to come back and clean them up, you know. Sometimes they'd go to a second day. But mostly, we always tried to... We played sometimes overtime, to get the record like it's supposed to be, like in... Of course, we didn't get paid for overtime. You just tried to complete the record.
I see. That meant, of course, that any rehearsing of the tune took place there, unless you rehearsed it well enough before you got to the studio.

Well, see, King Oliver always liked to rehearse when you get to the studio. It's better to rehearse it in the studio than it would before you get there, because if you rehearse before you get there, what you rehearse... We did a lot of rehearsing, say, about twice a week, before the recording, before you went on the road...
But the way we played the rehearsals uptown, it's a different sound altogether than when we'd get in the studio.
